newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina water bond bill contains safeguards.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina water bond bill contains safeguards.

text.p: The $1 billion water-sewer bond bill pending in North Carolina contains several provisions designed to ensure that the local government portion of the debt is repaid, the proposal's sponsor said Thursday.

Under the proposal by Sen. John Kerr, D-Wayne, $800 million of bond proceeds would be available to cities and counties to upgrade water, sewer and waste treatment systems. The remaining $200 million would be used to boost the state's existing revolving loan fund for clean water projects and to meet matching requirements for federal grants.
Before municipalities could draw from the $800 million portion, they would have to establish rates sufficient to make debt service payments, Kerr said.
"They would have to prove they could cover it," Kerr said.
The bill also authorizes the state to intercept municipalities' share of state revenues to make the debt service payment if necessary, Kerr said.
The bill was approved earlier this week by the Senate Finance Committee and is now pending in the appropriations committee. If approved by the General Assembly, it would go before voters in November.

The proposal would be the third major general obligation bond authorization in a little over a year in North Carolina. Voters approved $1.8 billion of school GOs and $950 million of highway GOs in November.
Kerr said the plan would not significantly boost the state's debt obligation, since the $800 million portion would be repaid by local governments.
"The state would still have to show it on a balance sheet, but its mostly a pass-through," Kerr said.
He said the bill had support from environmentalists, local governments and building developers and was expected to pass.

He said the pass-through funding portion would be used mainly by small towns and municipalities. Two-thirds of North Carolina's 527 municipalities and five of its counties have no bond ratings, or have ratings so low that borrowing costs would be prohibitive, he said.
"We've got so many small towns with 500 people, a thousand, 2,000," Kerr said. "The poor part of the state just cannot use private financing."
The proposal would enable them to reduce borrowing costs by taking advantage of the state's triple-A bond rating and would eliminate most of the cost of issuance by consolidating the debt, he said.
